title: Where are the single points of failure in this design, and how would you remove them?
summary: A design-review-style probe: can you scan a diagram and spot every unreplicated component, not just the obvious ones.

slides.markdown:
This is often asked right after you draw your first diagram — the interviewer is checking whether you can look at your own design critically and spot every component that would take down the whole system if it failed, not just the obvious one.

A **single point of failure (SPOF)** is anything with a count of one on the critical path. By the end of this topic you'll be able to scan a diagram systematically and name a concrete fix for each SPOF you find, including the ones fixes can accidentally create.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: none needed — this is a diagram exercise
slides.markdown:
Unlike most system-design questions, this one usually needs **no clarifying questions** — it's asking you to scan the diagram you (or the interviewer) already drew and find the weak points in it, not to gather new requirements.

The move here isn't to ask questions, it's to **narrate your scan out loud**: "let me walk through each box and check whether it's replicated." That narration is itself part of the signal — it shows a systematic process, not a lucky guess.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: walk the diagram, flag any count of one
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: walk the diagram **left to right** (or however the request flows), and for every box, ask **"is there only one of these?"** A single load balancer, a single database primary, a single cache node, a single "do everything" service that every other component calls — each is a SPOF until proven otherwise.

Doing this out loud, box by box, is more convincing than jumping straight to "the database is a SPOF" — it shows the method, not just a memorized answer about databases.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the classic three — LB, primary DB, and the one service everything calls
slides.markdown:
![A request-flow diagram with three components each highlighted as a single point of failure with a count of one: a load balancer, an auth service every other service calls, and a database primary](assets/spof-diagram.svg)

The database is the obvious one candidates name first. The load balancer and the shared dependency (often an auth or config service) are the ones that get missed — and missing them is the most common gap in this answer.

assets.alt: A request-flow diagram with three components each highlighted as a single point of failure with a count of one: a load balancer, an auth service every other service calls, and a database primary

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: fixing the load balancer
slides.markdown:
A single load balancer is a SPOF for the entire system — if it dies, nothing gets through, no matter how redundant everything behind it is. The standard fix: an **active-passive pair** behind a floating virtual IP (VIP) that fails over automatically, or **DNS-based failover** pointing at a healthy LB if the primary stops responding.

Name the failover time honestly — VIP failover is typically seconds, DNS failover can be much slower due to caching — since "fixed" doesn't mean "instant."

The standard fix for a single database primary: a **standby replica with automated failover** — a monitor detects the primary is unhealthy and promotes the replica, redirecting traffic to it.

Named cost to include: this has a real **RPO (recovery point objective)** — any writes that hadn't replicated to the standby at the moment of failure are lost. Saying "we might lose the last few seconds of writes, and here's how we'd bound that" is a stronger answer than implying the fix is lossless.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: fixing the hot dependency
slides.markdown:
A "one service everything calls" — often auth, config, or a shared lookup service — is a subtler SPOF, since it's easy to design and never revisit once it works. Two real fixes: **decouple it with a queue** so callers don't block synchronously on it, or add a **fallback path** (a cached last-known-good answer, or a degraded default) for when it's unreachable.

Either fix trades some freshness or correctness for availability — say which one you're choosing and why.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: not every SPOF is worth fixing
slides.markdown:
| SPOF | Fix cost | Typical priority |
|---|---|---|
| Load balancer | Low — active-passive pair, well-understood pattern | Fix almost always |
| Database primary | Medium — replica + failover automation + RPO tuning | Fix almost always |
| Internal batch/reporting job | Low value if it fails — usually just reruns later | Often not worth the extra infra |
| Rarely-used admin tool | Low blast radius, low traffic | Usually acceptable to leave as-is |

**How to decide:** weigh blast radius and frequency against fix cost — removing every SPOF adds real infrastructure and operational surface, and not all of them justify it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: which SPOF is cheapest to fix, and which is hardest?
slides.markdown:
Generally: the **load balancer** is cheapest — active-passive failover is a well-understood, off-the-shelf pattern. The **database** is harder — failover automation, replication lag, and RPO/RTO tuning take real engineering care to get right without introducing split-brain risk.

A shared internal dependency (auth, config) often sits in between — decoupling it with a queue or cache is straightforward, but finding every caller that assumed synchronous availability can be a larger, quieter effort than it first appears.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: did fixing the DB just move the SPOF to your failover coordinator?
slides.markdown:
Yes, often — and naming this is a senior-level detail. The tool that **detects the primary is down and promotes the replica** (a consensus service, a health-check daemon) is now itself on the critical path. If it's a single instance, you've traded one SPOF for another, just one layer removed.

The real fix is making the coordinator itself redundant (e.g. a small consensus cluster like etcd or ZooKeeper) — SPOFs can hide recursively inside the mechanism meant to remove them.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: naming only the database and missing the LB or a shared cache
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The database is the single point of failure" is a complete answer.

**Why it's wrong:** it's the SPOF everyone remembers to name, which means naming only it signals a shallow, one-pass scan rather than a systematic walk of the diagram. Load balancers, shared caches, and "the one service everyone calls" are just as real, and are the ones most often missed.

**Correct model:** scan every box on the diagram, not just the one that's easy to remember — narrate the walk so the interviewer sees the process, not just the conclusion.
